items.title: AI certificates are losing value; working projects now win jobs
points: Notes on AI competency in job applications have tripled for technical roles and quadrupled for other roles, but hiring managers now skip generic 'proficient in AI tools' claims much like they skip 'MS Office skills'.
Recruiters increasingly test an actual working tool rather than trust a certificate, which only proves course completion.
Engineering leaders ask candidates to walk through their project code and explain what the AI generated versus what they personally fixed, exposing those who don't understand their own work.

items.title: Case study: AI video editor project leads to ₹50 lakh job offers via direct outreach
points: A college student and co-founder spent two years building an AI video editor that plateaued at 13,000 users with no growth.
Despite the stall, the project led to two job offers worth ₹50 lakh annually—neither sourced through job portals.

The first offer came after a startup founder spotted the project on Twitter; the second came after the student emailed 30 similar companies, got 13 responses, and received an offer from a Y Combinator-backed startup within a week.

items.title: No-code portfolio built in a week using AI tools
points: A BBA student with zero coding experience built a portfolio website using Claude (an AI chatbot/assistant) and OpenCode (an AI coding tool).
He set clear rules for the AI and acted as quality assurance (QA, i.e., testing the output for errors) rather than writing code himself.
The project shows that non-technical people can ship working software in about a week by directing AI tools carefully.

items.title: 7-Day Build Challenge: a framework for demonstrating real AI skill
points: Day 1: find a specific person with a repetitive weekly problem (e.g., UPI payment matching, application sorting) and document current time spent.
Days 2–4: write 10 test cases, including edge cases (like Hinglish text or missing values), then build incrementally with AI, saving each working version and logging prompts versus personal edits.
Day 5: run all 10 tests, document failures and fixes, including cases where the AI claimed something worked but it didn't.
Day 6: have the original person use the tool, measure time saved (e.g., 45 minutes cut to 10), and record a 90-second screen walkthrough showing functionality and one caught bug.
Day 7: post publicly on LinkedIn/X and directly email 10 relevant founders or hiring managers describing the specific problem solved and who benefited, instead of sending a generic job application.

headlines: AI certificates are becoming job-market commodities while building working projects—even those you can't fully explain—now matters more to recruiters
A college student's two-year-old AI video editor that stalled at 13,000 users still landed him ₹50 lakh job offers, bypassing job portals entirely through Twitter and direct outreach
Interviewers increasingly ask candidates to walk through projects and explain what AI generated versus what they changed, exposing candidates who can't defend their work
A BBA student with zero coding experience built a portfolio site using Claude and OpenCode by setting clear rules and acting as QA, showing you can ship in a week with AI tools
The real differentiator is solving a concrete problem for someone—reducing a 45-minute task to 10 minutes with working code—which beats generic skill claims every time

sections.title: Why Projects Trump Certificates
points: 1. Notes on AI competency in job applications have tripled for technical roles and quadrupled for other roles, yet hiring managers skip past generic 'proficient in AI tools' claims the same way they skip 'MS Office skills'
2. Recruiters and founders can actually test a working tool to evaluate your real capabilities, whereas a certificate proves only that you completed a course

3. Engineering leaders now ask candidates to walk through projects, explain the code, and identify what the AI generated versus what they fixed—hiring managers can spot when you don't understand your own work in interviews

sections.title: The Case Study: Direct Outreach Works
points: 1. A college student built an AI video editor over two years with a co-founder; it never found growth beyond 13,000 users, yet generated two job offers at ₹50 lakh annually

2. First offer came from a startup founder who discovered it on Twitter; second came after he directly emailed 30 similar companies, received 13 responses, and got an offer from a Y Combinator-backed startup within a week
3. Neither offer came through job portals—direct evidence that a working product + personal outreach beats traditional hiring channels

sections.title: The 7-Day Build Challenge
points: 1. Day 1: Identify a specific person with a repetitive weekly problem (UPI payment matching, application sorting) and document the current time investment

2. Days 2–4: Write 10 test cases (including edge cases like Hinglish text or missing values), then build incrementally using AI, saving every working version and logging what you asked the AI to do and what you changed
3. Day 5: Run all 10 tests, find failures, fix them, and document exactly how you caught mistakes that the AI initially claimed worked
4. Day 6: Have the original person use it and measure the time saved (ideally 45 minutes down to 10); record a 90-second screen walkthrough showing functionality and one bug you caught
5. Day 7: Post on LinkedIn or X and email 10 relevant founders/hiring managers with the problem statement and who benefited—not a generic job application
